obstructive apnea produces less decrease in cardiac output and less left ventricular dysfunction than does central apnea.
in the sedated anesthetized pig, central apnea produces a more pronounced decrease in cardiac output than obstructive apnea, despite a comparable decrease in intrathoracic volume.
central apneas produced greater depression of cardiac output and greater changes of left ventricular afterload-related dysfunction than did obstructive apneas in anesthetized pigs.

the effects of apnea on the heart and circulation in sedated animals and humans.
the mechanisms of cardiovascular dysfunction associated with sleep-disordered breathing.
the cardiovascular response to periodic obstructive apnea.

the hemodynamic effects of obstructive and simulated apneas are not the same and that obstructive and central apneas are not equivalent in their hemodynamic effects.

the hemodynamic effects of apneas are determined by the interplay of several factors, including the duration of apneas, the magnitude and pattern of changes in intrathoracic and intrapleural pressures, and the magnitude of changes in arterial and venous blood gases.

the effects of apnea on the heart are complex and that the effects of obstructive and central apnea on the cardiovascular system are not equivalent.
central apnea is associated with greater changes in LV function and CO compared to obstructive apnea.
